bnqZzhIv544.title: My Maxims, Part 6
bnqZzhIv544.one_line: Eight months into Gaza, he urges the community to back student encampments, support those who act without demanding full agreement, and carry its weight.
bnqZzhIv544.summary: Although billed as the sixth talk in his maxims series, he sets the maxims aside and speaks about Gaza eight months into the bombardment. Every generation has a blind spot, he argues, and this is ours, so being able to see truth as truth is a blessing that brings responsibility. He points to an unprecedented shift in public opinion, especially among young people who no longer heed their parents' advice to keep their heads down, and to the campus encampments. Causes are won when public opinion moves first, and narratives change in academia, so those tied to Western University should keep up the pressure and the community must physically, financially and morally back students who are risking their futures. Recalling his second maxim, he insists you do not need to agree with someone completely to stand with them, and that Muslims who act are too often left to burn alone. Drawing on the Quran's picture of the hypocrite as a freeloader who takes the perks without the buy-in, he says every Muslim, aged 10 or 90, must find a role, and that Jumuah exists to deliver a message that demands action. In the second khutbah he calls this rare global Muslim unity a wave from Allah that must be turned into organized work before the nafs lets it fade.

outline.heading: Opening
Gaza as this generation's blind spot
outline.gist: Eight months of bombardment and over 30,000 dead, mostly women and children, while the world debates its legitimacy. Every era has a blind spot; being able to see right as right is a blessing to be grateful for.

outline.heading: An unprecedented shift in public opinion
outline.gist: Muslims must be a voice for the voiceless. With the International Court of Justice ordering a ceasefire in Rafah, he has never seen opinion shift so sharply, especially among the young.

outline.heading: Causes are won when public opinion moves first
outline.gist: Keeping the momentum is a responsibility before Allah. Before the world wars, enough awareness had to build before anything changed politically; political change may still be far off, but public opinion is there.

outline.heading: The young no longer walk beside the wall
outline.gist: Fifteen years ago parents would have stopped the encampments. He was raised in Syria to keep his head down and stay out of politics; today's students are not listening to that fear, and advice given out of fear can be taken with a grain of salt.

outline.heading: Encampments succeed when the community stands behind them
outline.gist: The successful encampments in the US, Canada and Europe had people bringing food, wisdom and physical presence. London's students are risking degrees and careers, and we owe it to them to show up.

outline.heading: Keep pressing Western
outline.gist: Beyond showing up, those affiliated with the university should keep up the pressure. Almost every household here is tied to it, and academic institutions carry weight in the world.

outline.heading: Narratives change in academia, not from the minbar
outline.gist: One well-published PhD thesis moves politics more than a lifetime of khutbahs, so academics and people of wealth and status should push the issue and protect the students.

outline.heading: Those who act are left to burn
outline.gist: Muslims who stick their necks out often lose everything while the community looks away, and the youth learn never to speak up.

outline.heading: Maxim 2 again: support without full agreement
outline.gist: You will never agree with anyone 100 percent. Zoom out to the broad strokes and stand with your brothers and sisters even when their methods are not yours.

outline.heading: Withdrawing over a refused request is shameful
outline.gist: Staying home because your requested change did not happen means everyone must dance to please you. Ask whether we stand for justice and the oppressed; if so, the details can wait.

outline.heading: Mistakes are part of the process: the companions
outline.gist: The companions made many mistakes and lost battles, but agreement on why they acted kept them together; without that mentality Islam would not have come this far.

outline.heading: Gaza has quieted our disagreements
outline.gist: Over eight months people have come to see what they share; the disagreements that glared last September are less visible because everyone is focused on a bigger picture.

outline.heading: The double standard
outline.gist: Supremacist rhetoric from a country everyone backs is played down, though a Muslim saying the same with the target changed would be arrested. Ending it requires communities to unite behind those taking action.

outline.heading: Not everyone can march, but everyone carries weight
outline.gist: If you cannot go to the encampment, support it another way. This applies to everything in your deen and ummah: carry your weight.

outline.heading: The hypocrite is a freeloader
outline.gist: From his Sunday tafsir: the Quran's munafiq takes the perks of being Muslim without the buy-in, giving no time, wealth or effort.

outline.heading: The Prophet's count and the missing 600
outline.gist: Knowing he had about 1,500 able to bear arms, the Prophet called and 900 came. The gap between the count and the output is the freeloaders, who want only to pray and leave.

outline.heading: Jumuah is not about attendance
outline.gist: At university in Syria students called themselves slaves of the attendance mark. Jumuah is obligatory because its message must be heard and acted on, so each person can find a role.

outline.heading: Find your role: on the wagon or under it
outline.gist: Whether 10 or 90, everyone has a role and will be asked about it. Either you carry the ummah with everyone else or it carries you.

outline.heading: Interlude
Gaza has united Muslims as Syria did not
outline.gist: Muslims failed to unite over many clear injustices, including Syria's destruction and seven million displaced, but have come together over Gaza. Allah has brought hearts together.

outline.heading: Turn unity into work
outline.gist: The momentum must become commitment, organizing, advocacy and education for the next generation. This is not feeding off suffering but using what has happened as fuel.

outline.heading: Plan the next steps for the students
outline.gist: Use the unity to bring Islam back to the front despite racial and cultural differences, support the students and talk seriously about how to apply more pressure.

outline.heading: Courage is rising; do not be petty
outline.gist: People now say on social media what once cost them their accounts, because not everyone can be cancelled. He disagrees with much in the community but refuses to be an obstacle.

outline.heading: A historic wave from Allah
outline.gist: Keep it moving and criticize later. Muslims have been weak for some 300 years; unlike 1948, technology now lets Muslims across the globe hear one another, and only giving up can stop it.

outline.heading: The nafs that wants things quiet
outline.gist: The part of you that wants this to die down so you can return to trips and comfort is the nafs. Ignore it and let the strength Allah put in your spirit rise.

outline.heading: Outro

5:25.en: [Moses] said, "My Lord, indeed I do not possess except myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people

5:26.ar: قَالَ فَإِنَّهَا مُحَرَّمَةٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡۛ أَرۡبَعِينَ سَنَةࣰۛ يَتِيهُونَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ فَلَا تَأۡسَ عَلَى ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ

11:87.en: They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worship or not do with our wealth what we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning

11:113.ar: وَلَا تَرۡكَنُوٓاْ إِلَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ فَتَمَسَّكُمُ ٱلنَّارُ وَمَا لَكُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ مِنۡ أَوۡلِيَآءَ ثُمَّ لَا تُنصَرُونَ
11:113.en: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest you be touched by the Fire, and you would not have other than Allah any protectors; then you would not be helped

11:62.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰصَٰلِحُ قَدۡ كُنتَ فِينَا مَرۡجُوࣰّ ا قَبۡلَ هَٰذَآۖ أَتَنۡهَىٰنَآ أَن نَّعۡبُدَ مَا يَعۡبُدُ ءَابَآؤُنَا وَإِنَّنَا لَفِي شَكࣲّ مِّمَّا تَدۡعُونَآ إِلَيۡهِ مُرِيبࣲ‏
11:62.en: They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of promise before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? And indeed we are, about that to which you invite us, in disquieting doubt

11:27.ar: فَقَالَ ٱلۡمَلَأُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مِن قَوۡمِهِۦ مَا نَرَىٰكَ إِلَّا بَشَرࣰ ا مِّثۡلَنَا وَمَا نَرَىٰكَ ٱتَّبَعَكَ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ هُمۡ أَرَاذِلُنَا بَادِيَ ٱلرَّأۡيِ وَمَا نَرَىٰ لَكُمۡ عَلَيۡنَا مِن فَضۡلِۭ بَلۡ نَظُنُّكُمۡ كَٰذِبِينَ
11:27.en: So the eminent among those who disbelieved from his people said, "We do not see you but as a man like ourselves, and we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us [and] at first suggestion. And we do not see in you over us any merit; rather, we think you are liars

11:28.ar: قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ أَرَءَيۡتُمۡ إِن كُنتُ عَلَىٰ بَيِّنَةࣲ مِّن رَّبِّي وَءَاتَىٰنِي رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّنۡ عِندِهِۦ فَعُمِّيَتۡ عَلَيۡكُمۡ أَنُلۡزِمُكُمُوهَا وَأَنتُمۡ لَهَا كَٰرِهُونَ
11:28.en: He said, "O my people have you considered: if I should be upon clear evidence from my Lord while He has given me mercy from Himself but it has been made unapparent to you, should we force it upon you while you are averse to it

11:29.ar: وَيَٰقَوۡمِ لَآ أَسۡـَٔلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ مَالًاۖ إِنۡ أَجۡرِيَ إِلَّا عَلَى ٱللَّهِۚ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ بِطَارِدِ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْۚ إِنَّهُم مُّلَٰقُواْ رَبِّهِمۡ وَلَٰكِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰكُمۡ قَوۡمࣰ ا تَجۡهَلُونَ
11:29.en: And O my people, I ask not of you for it any wealth. My reward is not but from Allah. And I am not one to drive away those who have believed. Indeed, they will meet their Lord, but I see that you are a people behaving ignorantly

PIAzoYYdAWM.title: My Maxims, Part 5
PIAzoYYdAWM.one_line: On the 76th Nakba anniversary, he argues Islam is reform, every prophet targeted his people's one deficit, and ours is passivity toward injustice.
PIAzoYYdAWM.summary: Marking 76 years since the Nakba, he criticizes the predictable Muslim response to Palestine: outrage and protests while bombs fall, then back to business as usual, which the other side has learned to simply outlast. Nothing lasts forever and the Holy Land was occupied longer before, so the question is not hope but what kind of generation will fix it. History shows only people who make justice their first priority, not a part-time interest, change their destiny, and they should expect no thanks except from Allah. Otherwise, like the Israelites who refused to follow Musa, the task waits for a later generation. Repeating last week's maxim that Islam without reform is not Islam, he shows from the stories of Shuayb, Lut, Hud, Salih and Nuh that each prophet confronted the one deficit of his people and refused to change the subject, and that people were judged by that deficit, not their other merits. The same holds personally: your story is what you are not doing right. In the second khutbah he explains the Quranic warning against growing comfortable with oppressors, criticizes rulers who love an Islam stripped of reform, and asks people to tie their personal and communal work to clear goals and to visit the Western encampment.

outline.heading: Opening
76 years since the Nakba
outline.gist: The Palestinians were driven from their land 76 years ago, and today the attempt to erase them from the land of their forefathers looks much like yesterday.

outline.heading: Our predictable outrage
outline.gist: Each bombing brings red faces, loud voices and a few weeks of protest, then business as usual with the companies and friends who back it. The other side has learned to simply outlast us.

outline.heading: No empowered group, no plan
outline.gist: It has stayed in the news only because the bombing has not stopped for eight months. No group has been given the community's full support to keep pushing, and no plan exists for when it ends.

outline.heading: The Holy Land was freed before
outline.gist: It was occupied for longer earlier in Islamic history and still freed, so there is no reason to lose hope. The question is what kind of generation will fix it.

outline.heading: A generation that puts righteousness first
outline.gist: Only people who treat justice and opposing oppression as priorities nothing trumps will change things. History shows no people ever freed themselves treating it as a part-time interest.

outline.heading: Give everything and expect no thanks
outline.gist: Those who changed their destiny gave everything without waiting for reward. No one will stand by you or thank you except Allah, and if we cannot accept that, we wait.

outline.heading: Musa and the forty years of wandering
outline.gist: Musa was ready but had only himself and Harun, so the land was forbidden to his people for forty years and the next generation entered it.

outline.heading: Then I will talk about something popular
outline.gist: Sarcastically he offers to preach on whatever people request instead. If righteousness does not trump everything and we will not speak against oppression, all this is a waste of time.

outline.heading: Live for it; you do not have to die for it
outline.gist: Others paid with their blood; we only have to direct our academic, social and financial lives toward strengthening the cause, which can be harder.

outline.heading: Restating the maxim: without reform Islam is not Islam
outline.gist: Reform means seeing where a people's problem is. Coming to a people with a deficit and talking about something else is a betrayal.

outline.heading: Shuayb's people ask two questions
outline.gist: They ask whether his prayer commands them to change whom they worship and what they do with their wealth. Every prophet began with tawhid, then the specific deficit.

outline.heading: Shuayb would not change the subject
outline.gist: He could have preached humility and kindness and become popular, but he kept naming their cheating with money until it was fixed.

outline.heading: Lut and Hud named their people's one problem
outline.gist: Lut addressed only the behaviour that had to stop; Hud confronted the racism and arrogance of Ad, not finances, because that was their problem.

outline.heading: This generation will be asked about injustice
outline.gist: We will be questioned about the injustices we witnessed and did little about, and listing other good deeds will not answer that question.

outline.heading: Judged by the deficit, not the merits
outline.gist: Shuayb's people were judged by their finances, not their manners, and destroyed when they did not fix it. A community's other merits are Allah's gifts anyway.

outline.heading: Your story is what you are not doing right
outline.gist: Personally, your story is what you know you are not doing right. No presentation of your strengths will help, since the rest was given to you; that weak spot is what you will be asked about.

outline.heading: Not wealth or numbers but willpower
outline.gist: We focus on other things and feel ashamed only while the bombing lasts. In 76 years Muslim communities have built no advocacy with teeth; the lack is willpower, commitment and understanding of what we will be judged on.

outline.heading: Interlude
Do not grow comfortable with oppressors
outline.gist: The verse near the end of Surah Hud forbids growing chummy with wrongdoers, or the Fire will touch you and no one will stand by you. Stand clearly against what you know is oppressive.

outline.heading: Salih and Hud fought one issue each
outline.gist: Study the Quran through the prophets' stories: each fought his people on one issue. Salih's people said they had hopes for him until he called out their wastefulness; Hud told Ad to stop oppressing others and being racist.

outline.heading: Nuh would not dismiss his poor followers
outline.gist: After 950 years his people offered to believe if he removed the lowly or held separate sessions for rich and poor. He compromised on everything but that.

outline.heading: Our deficit: letting injustice slide
outline.gist: Equality was the deficit Nuh came to fix. Ours is that injustices keep happening while we take no clear stand against them and let too much slide.

outline.heading: Dictators love Islam without reform
outline.gist: We are normalizing what the Quran forbids. Rulers are happy with bigger masjids, better sound systems and full rows as long as no one speaks against dictatorship or corruption.

outline.heading: Syria: anything but oppression
outline.gist: Living in Syria he could speak about anything except the glaring oppression, and that version of religion failed. Speaking out must cost us, or we wander for forty years.

outline.heading: Why not this generation
outline.gist: One generation will do it, so start the push now even if we never see the result. Education, mentorship and outreach continue, but tied to clearly defined goals.

outline.heading: Back the students at Western
outline.gist: Drop in to show solidarity with the encampment. Help that age group believe it can make a difference, and give it experienced counsel.

outline.heading: Outro

28:14.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥ وَٱسۡتَوَىٰٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
28:14.en: And when he attained his full strength and was [mentally] mature, We bestowed upon him judgement and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good

28:15.ar: وَدَخَلَ ٱلۡمَدِينَةَ عَلَىٰ حِينِ غَفۡلَةࣲ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِهَا فَوَجَدَ فِيهَا رَجُلَيۡنِ يَقۡتَتِلَانِ هَٰذَا مِن شِيعَتِهِۦ وَهَٰذَا مِنۡ عَدُوِّهِۦۖ فَٱسۡتَغَٰثَهُ ٱلَّذِي مِن شِيعَتِهِۦ عَلَى ٱلَّذِي مِنۡ عَدُوِّهِۦ فَوَكَزَهُۥ مُوسَىٰ فَقَضَىٰ عَلَيۡهِۖ قَالَ هَٰذَا مِنۡ عَمَلِ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِۖ إِنَّهُۥ عَدُوࣱّ مُّضِلࣱّ مُّبِينࣱ‏
28:15.en: And he entered the city at a time of inattention by its people and found therein two men fighting: one from his faction and one from among his enemy. And the one from his faction called for help to him against the one from his enemy, so Moses struck him and [unintentionally] killed him. [Moses] said, "This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is a manifest, misleading enemy

28:16.ar: قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي ظَلَمۡتُ نَفۡسِي فَٱغۡفِرۡ لِي فَغَفَرَ لَهُۥٓۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلۡغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
28:16.en: He said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful

28:17.ar: قَالَ رَبِّ بِمَآ أَنۡعَمۡتَ عَلَيَّ فَلَنۡ أَكُونَ ظَهِيرࣰ ا لِّلۡمُجۡرِمِينَ
28:17.en: He said, "My Lord, for the favor You bestowed upon me, I will never be an assistant to the criminals

28:18.ar: فَأَصۡبَحَ فِي ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ خَآئِفࣰ ا يَتَرَقَّبُ فَإِذَا ٱلَّذِي ٱسۡتَنصَرَهُۥ بِٱلۡأَمۡسِ يَسۡتَصۡرِخُهُۥۚ قَالَ لَهُۥ مُوسَىٰٓ إِنَّكَ لَغَوِيࣱّ مُّبِينࣱ‏
28:18.en: And he became inside the city fearful and anticipating [exposure], when suddenly the one who sought his help the previous day cried out to him [once again]. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are an evident, [persistent] deviator

28:19.ar: فَلَمَّآ أَنۡ أَرَادَ أَن يَبۡطِشَ بِٱلَّذِي هُوَ عَدُوࣱّ لَّهُمَا قَالَ يَٰمُوسَىٰٓ أَتُرِيدُ أَن تَقۡتُلَنِي كَمَا قَتَلۡتَ نَفۡسَۢا بِٱلۡأَمۡسِۖ إِن تُرِيدُ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ جَبَّارࣰ ا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَمَا تُرِيدُ أَن تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُصۡلِحِينَ
28:19.en: And when he wanted to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them, he said, "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed someone yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land and do not want to be of the amenders

40:34.ar: وَلَقَدۡ جَآءَكُمۡ يُوسُفُ مِن قَبۡلُ بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ فَمَا زِلۡتُمۡ فِي شَكࣲّ مِّمَّا جَآءَكُم بِهِۦۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا هَلَكَ قُلۡتُمۡ لَن يَبۡعَثَ ٱللَّهُ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ رَسُولࣰ اۚ كَذَٰلِكَ يُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ مَنۡ هُوَ مُسۡرِفࣱ مُّرۡتَابٌ
40:34.en: And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt of that which he brought to you, until when he died, you said, 'Never will Allah send a messenger after him.' Thus does Allah leave astray he who is a transgressor and skeptic

6:159.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ فَرَّقُواْ دِينَهُمۡ وَكَانُواْ شِيَعࣰ ا لَّسۡتَ مِنۡهُمۡ فِي شَيۡءٍۚ إِنَّمَآ أَمۡرُهُمۡ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا كَانُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
6:159.en: Indeed, those who have divided their religion and become sects - you, [O Muhammad], are not [associated] with them in anything. Their affair is only [left] to Allah; then He will inform them about what they used to do

40:28.ar: وَقَالَ رَجُلࣱ مُّؤۡمِنࣱ مِّنۡ ءَالِ فِرۡعَوۡنَ يَكۡتُمُ إِيمَٰنَهُۥٓ أَتَقۡتُلُونَ رَجُلًا أَن يَقُولَ رَبِّيَ ٱللَّهُ وَقَدۡ جَآءَكُم بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ مِن رَّبِّكُمۡۖ وَإِن يَكُ كَٰذِبࣰ ا فَعَلَيۡهِ كَذِبُهُۥۖ وَإِن يَكُ صَادِقࣰ ا يُصِبۡكُم بَعۡضُ ٱلَّذِي يَعِدُكُمۡۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي مَنۡ هُوَ مُسۡرِفࣱ كَذَّابࣱ‏
40:28.en: And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith said, "Do you kill a man [merely] because he says, 'My Lord is Allah' while he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he should be lying, then upon him is [the consequence of] his lie; but if he should be truthful, there will strike you some of what he promises you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar

4:34.ar: ٱلرِّجَالُ قَوَّٰمُونَ عَلَى ٱلنِّسَآءِ بِمَا فَضَّلَ ٱللَّهُ بَعۡضَهُمۡ عَلَىٰ بَعۡضࣲ وَبِمَآ أَنفَقُواْ مِنۡ أَمۡوَٰلِهِمۡۚ فَٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ قَٰنِتَٰتٌ حَٰفِظَٰتࣱ لِّلۡغَيۡبِ بِمَا حَفِظَ ٱللَّهُۚ وَٱلَّٰتِي تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَٱهۡجُرُوهُنَّ فِي ٱلۡمَضَاجِعِ وَٱضۡرِبُوهُنَّۖ فَإِنۡ أَطَعۡنَكُمۡ فَلَا تَبۡغُواْ عَلَيۡهِنَّ سَبِيلًاۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيࣰّ ا كَبِيرࣰ ا
4:34.en: Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allah would have them guard. But those [wives] from whom you fear arrogance - [first] advise them; [then if they persist], forsake them in bed; and [finally], strike them. But if they obey you [once more], seek no means against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Grand

21:87.ar: وَذَا ٱلنُّونِ إِذ ذَّهَبَ مُغَٰضِبࣰ ا فَظَنَّ أَن لَّن نَّقۡدِرَ عَلَيۡهِ فَنَادَىٰ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ أَن لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
21:87.en: And [mention] the man of the fish, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decree [anything] upon him. And he called out within the darknesses, "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers

21:88.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ وَنَجَّيۡنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلۡغَمِّۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُـۨجِي ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ

WWhSX1Fs9pQ.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat al-Qasas, Musa Strikes the Egyptian (28:14-19)
WWhSX1Fs9pQ.one_line: Musa's killing of the Egyptian: anger, taking responsibility instead of blaming Shaytan, refusing to back criminals, and standing by a troublesome people.
WWhSX1Fs9pQ.summary: He recalls that al-Qasas teaches we cannot judge others' complex stories, though their motives are simple, and that Islam often joins things that seem opposed, like full effort and full reliance. The real revolution is against one's own self: ask why you act, not why others do, and distinguish judging an act from judging a person. Musa matured with judgement and knowledge; the young companions who had both carried Islam after the Prophet, so we must raise youth with encouragement, as the Prophet did with Ibn Abbas. Musa visited his enslaved people at night; long tyranny had corrupted their morals, so they deserve mercy, and he worked for a generation he would not see succeed. His single punch killed the Egyptian; calling it Shaytan's work does not shift blame but admits anger exceeded its measure, so feelings must not drive actions. He then owns the wrong, asks forgiveness, and vows never to support criminals, though palace life offered him power. He refused to answer oppression with revenge on innocents. When the same Israelite fights again, Musa calls him misguided yet still stands with him against the oppressor, and this time he restrains himself. Our own communities have many faults, but we must not abandon them for polished tyrants. He closes with the supplication of Yunus as a remedy for distress.

outline.heading: Opening
Relationships fill human life
outline.gist: Caring for relationships makes people happier; the axis ends with as-Sajdah, the relationship with Allah.

outline.heading: Recap: complex stories, simple motives
outline.gist: Al-Qasas shows in every story that we cannot judge people, yet their stories are simple at root.

outline.heading: Islam joins what seems opposed: tawakkul
outline.gist: Reliance means full effort with full dependence on Allah; likewise, see every decision of yours as driven by simple motives like vanity or envy.

outline.heading: A revolution against the self
outline.gist: We question others' motives, never our own; Allah made us responsible for our own heart, not for judging others' intentions.

outline.heading: Judging the act versus judging the person
outline.gist: You may judge that an act is wrong; judging the person's state is another matter entirely.

outline.heading: Recitation: the fight in the city
outline.gist: The story of Musa continues to about verse forty, each step showing outward and inward differ.

outline.heading: Returned in honour, raised in the palace
outline.gist: Pharaoh paid for his rival's nursing; Musa matured and gained standing, unlike Yusuf who was then a slave.

outline.heading: Judgement and knowledge: without them a generation is lost
outline.gist: Hukm is the ability to decide and tell right from wrong, 'ilm is understanding and learning from experience.

outline.heading: Young companions carried Islam forward
outline.gist: After the Prophet died and many apostatised, young people with judgement and knowledge carried the faith; when such people vanish, the Hour comes.

outline.heading: Raising youth: Ibn Abbas and the cup
outline.gist: Good manners do not mean silence; the Prophet encouraged the boy Ibn Abbas, and seeing in a youth what he cannot yet see lifts him.

outline.heading: Entering the city in a moment of heedlessness
outline.gist: A quiet hour such as midday or night when people were indoors, not a festival day.

outline.heading: Musa in Pharaoh's house after Asiya
outline.gist: Pharaoh disliked him but tolerated him; Musa knew who he was and cared for his people.

outline.heading: Enslavement corrupts a people's morals
outline.gist: Generations under tyranny and racism lost knowledge and manners; their bad conduct later in the story has this cause.

outline.heading: Mercy for those who had no choice; Musa's night visits
outline.gist: He went to his people at night to learn from their scholars and teach their children; they believed him later because they loved him before.

outline.heading: Patience for a generation you will not see
outline.gist: Musa, like the Prophet, did not see full success; real change takes a lifetime of patience.

outline.heading: The Israelites on the remnants of Yusuf's law
outline.gist: Enslavement brought innovation, shirk and superstition, but a remnant of Yusuf's teaching remained.

outline.heading: One of his own faction, one of his enemy
outline.gist: Not every Israelite was his; hypocrites from within do the most damage, while some Egyptians were believers.

outline.heading: Istighathah: literal and figurative
outline.gist: True rescue is sought only from Allah; seeking help from people is a figurative use within its own domain.

outline.heading: Questions that carry accusations
outline.gist: He rebukes those who object to saying 'may Allah be pleased with him' for Abu Hanifa and who question others' practice without the manners of a student.

outline.heading: Wakz: a closed-fist blow
outline.gist: Wakz is a punch; the word for striking in 4:34 cannot mean the full palm or fist.

outline.heading: This is Shaytan's work: anger beyond its measure
outline.gist: Musa did not intend to kill; he is not blaming Shaytan but saying Shaytan inflated his zeal and anger.

outline.heading: Do not get angry: do not act on feelings
outline.gist: Commands about emotions mean do not act on them; wait until anger passes, even anger for Allah, and turn it into a considered decision.

outline.heading: The kind of killing and Shaytan's open enmity
outline.gist: Killing with a weapon that usually kills differs from a blow that usually does not; Shaytan's job is enmity and misguidance.

outline.heading: Shaytan only whispers; the decision is ours
outline.gist: Shaytan's harm to us is only what we choose after his suggestion; the next verse proves Musa took the blame.

outline.heading: I wronged myself: blaming others is folly
outline.gist: Blaming others for your own acts is legal foolishness; a man who says his wife makes him angry might as well hand her the right of divorce.

outline.heading: By Your favour, I will never back the criminals
outline.gist: Grateful for being given judgement and knowledge others lacked, Musa vows never to support wrongdoers.

outline.heading: He could have been Pharaoh's intelligence chief
outline.gist: Raised in the palace he could have ruled over his people; Allah chooses prophets who could have chosen otherwise.

outline.heading: The people he would lead
outline.gist: The same people later worshipped the calf and told him to fight with his Lord alone, yet he bore them.

outline.heading: No revenge on the innocent
outline.gist: Musa regretted killing even an oppressor's man; killing any member of the oppressing people only increases blood and hatred.

outline.heading: Recitation of yastasrikhuhu
outline.gist: The emphatic sad must not swallow the letters around it; practice the four emphatic letters.

outline.heading: Fearful and watchful; you are clearly misguided
outline.gist: Musa knew he would get no fair trial; the same man calls again, and Musa names him ghawi, one who drifts into trouble.

outline.heading: Our own communities' faults
outline.gist: Muslim communities have bad manners and disputes, but the attitude that they are unworthy and the polished oppressor is better must change.

outline.heading: Musa stands with his people regardless
outline.gist: Even if all his people were misguided he stayed with them and stood with the wronged against the tyrant.

outline.heading: Fa-lamma an arada: he learned from the first time
outline.gist: The extra 'an' signals a pause; Musa held back his anger this time.

outline.heading: Never abandon your brother, even the troublemaker
outline.gist: Restrain him from wrongdoing but do not desert him; betrayal often comes from your own people, as the informer here did.

outline.heading: Interlude
The supplication of Yunus for distress
outline.gist: No Muslim calls with Yunus's words of tawhid and confession in any matter without Allah answering him.

63:7.en: They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disband." And to Allah belongs the depositories of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand

63:8.ar: يَقُولُونَ لَئِن رَّجَعۡنَآ إِلَى ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ لَيُخۡرِجَنَّ ٱلۡأَعَزُّ مِنۡهَا ٱلۡأَذَلَّۚ وَلِلَّهِ ٱلۡعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِۦ وَلِلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَلَٰكِنَّ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقِينَ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
63:8.en: They say, "If we return to al-Madinah, the more honored [for power] will surely expel therefrom the more humble." And to Allah belongs [all] honor, and to His Messenger, and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know

63:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تُلۡهِكُمۡ أَمۡوَٰلُكُمۡ وَلَآ أَوۡلَٰدُكُمۡ عَن ذِكۡرِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَمَن يَفۡعَلۡ ذَٰلِكَ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡخَٰسِرُونَ
63:9.en: O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that - then those are the losers

63:10.ar: وَأَنفِقُواْ مِن مَّا رَزَقۡنَٰكُم مِّن قَبۡلِ أَن يَأۡتِيَ أَحَدَكُمُ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ فَيَقُولَ رَبِّ لَوۡلَآ أَخَّرۡتَنِيٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلࣲ قَرِيبࣲ فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ

LhX1xqL3vdw.title: Surat Al-Munafiqun, Part 3 (Verses 8-11)
LhX1xqL3vdw.one_line: Al-Munafiqun 8-11: carrying your weight, Ibn Ubayy's racist threat and the Prophet's restraint, true honour, and two safeguards against hypocrisy.
LhX1xqL3vdw.summary: He recaps the surah's core claim that the community's real enemy is within: freeloaders who take every benefit and give nothing. Believers must beware of them without labelling, excluding or fighting anyone, and use the descriptions to examine themselves. Expeditions required each fighter to bring his own provisions, which he turns into a challenge for his own community: contribute time, skills or money to the masjid rather than treating it as a free service, and act in ways that would work if everyone did the same. Verse 8 tells the story of the quarrel at a well on the expedition, the Prophet's rebuke of tribal rallying calls as rotten, and Ibn Ubayy's boast that the mighty would expel the lowly from Madinah, which he calls collective arrogance, the essence of racism. The Prophet refused to have him killed, honoured his son, and later prayed over him, while the son barred his father from entering Madinah without the Prophet's permission. Honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers. The closing verses give two safeguards: do not let wealth and family distract you from the purpose you were created for, and give from whatever you have before death arrives and you beg for a little more time. He recommends imagining your own death to regain perspective.

outline.heading: Opening
Recap: the comprehensive surahs and the organizational cluster
outline.gist: Juz 28's surahs organize relationships among Muslims, with non-Muslims, the social contract, leadership and finally the hypocrites.

outline.heading: The true enemy comes from within
outline.gist: For the community as for the individual, the real problem is inside, not across the fence.

outline.heading: Beware, but never exclude or fight
outline.gist: Do not let freeloaders ruin your progress, but you may not remove them; Surat At-Tawbah gives the detail.

outline.heading: The carriage: pushers, riders and those pushing back
outline.gist: Most of the work is done by a tiny fraction while many simply ride along and take the perks.

outline.heading: Never label anyone a hypocrite
outline.gist: Even the Prophet did not expose those he knew; the descriptions are warnings for oneself, and hypocrisy is a spectrum.

outline.heading: No freeloading on expeditions
outline.gist: Fighters had to bring their own mount, food and shoes or stay behind excused, while the wealthy equipped others.

outline.heading: Carry your weight in the masjid
outline.gist: People use classes, funerals and the cemetery and show up for Eid prayers without contributing; he prefers not to charge but expects everyone to give time, skills or money.

outline.heading: Recap: withholding provisions to break the companions
outline.gist: The hypocrites refused to share when the expedition ran three times longer than planned.

outline.heading: Act as if everyone would copy you
outline.gist: Like pandemic hoarding, behaviour that would collapse the system if everyone did it makes you part of the problem.

outline.heading: Four kinds of people
outline.gist: The one who knows and knows it, knows but forgot it, is ignorant and knows it, and is ignorant without knowing; avoid the last.

outline.heading: Interlude
"The mightier will expel the lowlier"
outline.gist: Double emphasis in their threat, with Ibn Ubayy meaning himself and the Prophet and his followers.

outline.heading: The quarrel at the well: "Leave it, it is rotten"
outline.gist: A shove between a Muhajir and an Ansari became tribal rallying cries; the Prophet ran out half-dressed and condemned the calls of jahiliyyah that once fuelled decades of feuds.

outline.heading: Ibn Ubayy's insult, and racism as collective arrogance
outline.gist: He compared the Muslims to a dog that eats its feeder; believing one's group superior is arrogance multiplied.

outline.heading: The boy who reported it
outline.gist: Zayd ibn Arqam told the Prophet, who questioned him repeatedly to teach him not to spread such talk.

outline.heading: "Muhammad does not kill his companions"
outline.gist: Umar suggested execution; the Prophet refused and insisted on treating him well as long as he outwardly remained with them.

outline.heading: The son's offer
outline.gist: Abdullah, Ibn Ubayy's believing son, asked to carry out any execution himself rather than live seeing his father's killer; the Prophet again refused.

outline.heading: Forgiving the man whose crown he took
outline.gist: Despite twelve documented harms, the Prophet kept forgiving, then prayed over him and shrouded him in his own garment for his son's sake before revelation forbade it; death should end grudges.

outline.heading: Honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers
outline.gist: True honour is what lasts into eternity; hypocrites do not know where wealth and honour come from, so they hoard and ally with the strong.

outline.heading: Ask the elderly what mattered
outline.gist: People in their eighties and nineties say to live by what you believe is right, since life passes in a moment.

outline.heading: The son at the gate of Madinah
outline.gist: Abdullah barred his father from entering until the Prophet permitted it, and the Prophet told him to let his father in and treat him kindly.

outline.heading: Summary: the hypocrite's traits in the surah
outline.gist: Claims without commitment, polished surface, guilt, disrespect for the Prophet, withholding wealth and reviving tribal and national divisions; reflect on them in yourself.

outline.heading: Interlude
Lahw: being distracted from the priority
outline.gist: Distraction can be pointless fun or a worthwhile task at the wrong time, like tidying your room before an exam.

outline.heading: Wealth and children: financial and social support
outline.gist: Amwal and awlad stand for financial and social needs; no one in a Muslim community should be lonely, as distinct from alone.

outline.heading: Don't let the gifts distract from the purpose
outline.gist: Allah made the world for you and you for Him; enjoy wealth and family and use them to draw closer, not live for them.

outline.heading: The real losers, and families entering Paradise together
outline.gist: Those distracted by blessings lose them all; those who used them well find wealth and children waiting for them.

outline.heading: Give from what We provided
outline.gist: Rizq includes time, knowledge and skills; infaq, sharing a root with nifaq, is giving that disappears with nothing expected back.

outline.heading: Rehearse your own death
outline.gist: An early scholar would lie in a narrow space imagining his death, then rise saying he had another chance; the exercise brings perspective and joy.

outline.heading: "If only You delayed me": sadaqah proves the claim
outline.gist: The dying ask for a little time to give in charity; sadaqah is proof of truthfulness, answering the hypocrites' empty testimony.

outline.heading: No delay, and every breath is a second chance
outline.gist: When the term comes there is no extension; any time not guaranteed to you is a second chance.

outline.heading: Khabir: He knows the hidden truth
outline.gist: The closing name points to inner states only Allah knows; the two safeguards are not being distracted and giving now.

64:1.ar: يُسَبِّحُ لِلَّهِ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ وَلَهُ ٱلۡحَمۡدُۖ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرٌ
64:1.en: Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is exalting Allah. To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs [all] praise, and He is over all things competent

64:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكُمۡ فَمِنكُمۡ كَافِرࣱ وَمِنكُم مُّؤۡمِنࣱۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ
64:2.en: It is He who created you, and among you is the disbeliever, and among you is the believer. And Allah, of what you do, is Seeing

64:3.ar: خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَصَوَّرَكُمۡ فَأَحۡسَنَ صُوَرَكُمۡۖ وَإِلَيۡهِ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
64:3.en: He created the heavens and earth in truth and formed you and perfected your forms; and to Him is the [final] destination

64:4.ar: يَعۡلَمُ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَيَعۡلَمُ مَا تُسِرُّونَ وَمَا تُعۡلِنُونَۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
64:4.en: He knows what is within the heavens and earth and knows what you conceal and what you declare. And Allah is Knowing of that within the breasts

2:170.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ بَلۡ نَتَّبِعُ مَآ أَلۡفَيۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَنَآۚ أَوَلَوۡ كَانَ ءَابَآؤُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡقِلُونَ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يَهۡتَدُونَ
2:170.en: And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed," they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers doing." Even though their fathers understood nothing, nor were they guided

59:24.ar: هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡخَٰلِقُ ٱلۡبَارِئُ ٱلۡمُصَوِّرُۖ لَهُ ٱلۡأَسۡمَآءُ ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰۚ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ

Lx83VHAm9wE.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Taghabun, Part 1 (64:1-4)
Lx83VHAm9wE.one_line: Al-Taghabun as the reminder of why we act: exalting Allah, purposeful creation, and the intentions He knows behind every deed.
Lx83VHAm9wE.summary: He presents Al-Taghabun as a Madani surah with a Makki flavour, placed among technical, ruling-heavy surahs to remind believers why they do any of it. When practice loses its purpose of pleasing Allah it hardens into custom, like an engagement procession that has forgotten its role as a guarantee of accountability, and means such as a masjid or institution become ends in themselves, which is corruption. Taghabun, from deception in trade, names the day when it becomes clear who fooled whom. He explains tasbih as exalting Allah beyond any flaw, a level above praise that means never questioning Him, grounded in His kingship, praiseworthiness and power, and illustrates the harm of zeal without purpose with a Syrian story of two responses to a man who prayed only Fajr. Kufr is denying a blessing, above all creation, and belief is proven by how one lives. Creation bil-haqq means purposefully; through Al-Khaliq, Al-Bari and Al-Musawwir he argues that sawwara means giving purpose, not shaping appearance. People who know their purpose live differently, as the Prophet did, and emulating him counts most where it is hardest. Allah knows what is in the chests, so intention is decisive: act for Allah, not one's group, and ask whether you could bear never being thanked.

outline.heading: A Madani surah with a Makki flavour
outline.gist: Among the organizational Madani surahs, Al-Taghabun reads like a Makki surah in its wording and tone.

outline.heading: Purpose as the safety valve
outline.gist: Spiritual passages amid technical rulings keep the purpose of pleasing Allah in view, so practice never turns harmful or tribal.

outline.heading: Its place after the organizational surahs
outline.gist: After surahs on relationships, citizenship, the social contract, leadership and hypocrisy, this surah adds that without purpose everything collapses.

outline.heading: When practices become customs: following the fathers
outline.gist: Practices no longer measured against pleasing Allah mutate into culture, like Quraysh following their fathers without asking whether they were guided.

outline.heading: Empty rituals and the next generation
outline.gist: Rituals reduced to skeletons stop making people better, and the next generation walks away from them.

outline.heading: The engagement procession that forgot its purpose
outline.gist: The large group accompanying a proposal was meant to show both bride and groom have people they answer to; it became showing off, traffic jams and waste.

outline.heading: The meaning of taghabun
outline.gist: Ghabn is deception in trade through ignorance or concealment; the Day of Judgment is when it becomes clear who fooled whom.

outline.heading: When the means become the goal
outline.gist: Once an institution's survival matters more than its function, it is corrupt, as with a company that cuts quality just to survive.

outline.heading: The masjid is a means, not an end
outline.gist: The goal is education, mentorship, unity, outreach and advocacy; do not build or expand for its own sake.

outline.heading: The day all deceit fades
outline.gist: Those who thought they were fooling others will find themselves the ones fooled before Allah.

outline.heading: Interlude
The last opening of tasbih in the juz
outline.gist: The repeated openings of exaltation through these surahs are gathered and explained here.

outline.heading: Technicality without purpose breeds harshness
outline.gist: Those who think the purpose is doing it right yell at people in the masjid for mistakes, driving them away instead of pleasing Allah.

outline.heading: The man who prayed only Fajr
outline.gist: A Syrian story: one man scolded him until he quit; another praised him and added Dhuhr, remembering the goal.

outline.heading: Tasbih: exaltation beyond praise
outline.gist: Praise, respect and obedience can be given to people; exalting means declaring someone beyond any flaw we could identify, which is for Allah alone.

outline.heading: Exalting means never questioning Him
outline.gist: We do not hold Allah to account or ask for a break; everything else in creation exalts Him and humans alone choose.

outline.heading: To Him belongs all sovereignty and praise
outline.gist: Allah literally owns us, body and soul, unlike any human ownership, and is always worthy of praise.

outline.heading: Exaltation ties every command to its purpose
outline.gist: Because He is King, Praiseworthy and Omnipotent, His commands cannot be weighed like a ruler's and must be connected to the objectives He set.

outline.heading: Interlude
Kufr as denying a blessing
outline.gist: Kufr means covering or refusing to acknowledge a favour; denying the blessing of creation became synonymous with disbelief.

outline.heading: Al-Basir: belief proven by how you live
outline.gist: Whether one acknowledges the Creator shows in behaviour, which Allah sees.

outline.heading: Created bil-haqq: purposefully
outline.gist: Haqq here is the opposite of aimlessness: creation has a goal, a plot and an ending.

outline.heading: The other reading: creation runs on justice
outline.gist: Reading haqq as justice is valid elsewhere, but here the context points to purpose.

outline.heading: Al-Khaliq: from nothing to something
outline.gist: Creating from absolute nothingness, without time or space, is beyond human comprehension.

outline.heading: Al-Bari: from no life to life
outline.gist: Science studies how the universe and the first cell work, not where the first matter or life came from.

outline.heading: Al-Musawwir: the granter of purpose
outline.gist: Surah means a design with an objective; science cannot answer why every living thing wants to live, grow and survive.

outline.heading: Shaped for a purpose, not for looks
outline.gist: Our selfish earthly side and our selfless higher side, like a tree's form, exist to serve a purpose; translating sawwara as appearance is a poor reading.

outline.heading: Not about beauty: purpose for every person
outline.gist: Some are born with deformities, so the verse cannot mean beauty; our bodies and minds are made the way they are so we can achieve something.

outline.heading: People who know why they are here live differently
outline.gist: Returning to Allah forces the question of purpose; those who answer it value different things and work selflessly for decades.

outline.heading: The Prophet as a new paradigm of a human being
outline.gist: His opponents could find no selfish motive in him, so people either fled from him or attached themselves to him for life.

outline.heading: He made it look effortless
outline.gist: Like a grandmaster or a tennis player, he made his way of living look easy; try it and you find it is not.

outline.heading: Emulate him where it hurts
outline.gist: Following the Sunnah counts in the one difficult relationship, desire or fear you avoid, not only where it is easy.

outline.heading: Returning to Him: the widening circle of caregiving
outline.gist: As khalifah and servant, one's responsibility grows from self to siblings, spouse, children, parents and community.

outline.heading: Interlude
He knows what is in the chests
outline.gist: Allah knows what we hide and reveal, down to fleeting thoughts, fears and envy that never become actions.

outline.heading: The four verses as a portrait of Allah
outline.gist: Exalted, King, Praiseworthy, Omnipotent, Creator, Seer, purposeful Designer and All-Knowing, ending with knowledge of the heart.

outline.heading: Right deed, wrong reason, goes nowhere
outline.gist: A visible good deed must be built on selflessness, humility and love; arrogance or envy inside empties it.

outline.heading: A concise description of Allah amid a technical juz
outline.gist: No other part of the juz describes Allah so densely, so that we remember why we do all the rest.

outline.heading: Ask why you do what you do
outline.gist: If everyone asked who they are serving, behaviour and outcomes would change; what matters most is why something was done.

outline.heading: For Allah, not for my group
outline.gist: Once work is for one's race, nation or group it becomes the law of the jungle; for Allah it carries a higher moral standard.

outline.heading: The test: could you bear never being thanked?
outline.gist: If you need loyalty, votes or praise in return, say so honestly; doing it for Allah means wanting it never mentioned again.

outline.heading: Don't fool yourself
outline.gist: Doing things for Allah, by His teachings, protects communities from harm and arrogance, which is why the surah sits before the most technical one.

28:20.ar: وَجَآءَ رَجُلࣱ مِّنۡ أَقۡصَا ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ يَسۡعَىٰ قَالَ يَٰمُوسَىٰٓ إِنَّ ٱلۡمَلَأَ يَأۡتَمِرُونَ بِكَ لِيَقۡتُلُوكَ فَٱخۡرُجۡ إِنِّي لَكَ مِنَ ٱلنَّٰصِحِينَ

28:21.ar: فَخَرَجَ مِنۡهَا خَآئِفࣰ ا يَتَرَقَّبُۖ قَالَ رَبِّ نَجِّنِي مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
28:21.en: So he left it, fearful and anticipating [apprehension]. He said, "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people

28:22.ar: وَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلۡقَآءَ مَدۡيَنَ قَالَ عَسَىٰ رَبِّيٓ أَن يَهۡدِيَنِي سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ
28:22.en: And when he directed himself toward Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way

28:23.ar: وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَآءَ مَدۡيَنَ وَجَدَ عَلَيۡهِ أُمَّةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ يَسۡقُونَ وَوَجَدَ مِن دُونِهِمُ ٱمۡرَأَتَيۡنِ تَذُودَانِۖ قَالَ مَا خَطۡبُكُمَاۖ قَالَتَا لَا نَسۡقِي حَتَّىٰ يُصۡدِرَ ٱلرِّعَآءُۖ وَأَبُونَا شَيۡخࣱ كَبِيرࣱ‏
28:23.en: And when he came to the well of Madyan, he found there a crowd of people watering [their flocks], and he found aside from them two women driving back [their flocks]. He said, "What is your circumstance?" They said, "We do not water until the shepherds dispatch [their flocks]; and our father is an old man

28:24.ar: فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّىٰٓ إِلَى ٱلظِّلِّ فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَآ أَنزَلۡتَ إِلَيَّ مِنۡ خَيۡرࣲ فَقِيرࣱ‏

lPQ5K9UmUuA.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat al-Qasas, Musa Flees to Madyan (28:19-24)
lPQ5K9UmUuA.one_line: Musa flees Egypt for Madyan: siding with the oppressed, refusing to judge, leaving home without complaint, and the courtesy of helping two women.
lPQ5K9UmUuA.summary: He restates that judging others usually springs from suspicion and a wish to feel superior, while the motives behind any story are simple. Musa, raised in privilege, could have ruled over his people but stood with the oppressed against an oppressor whose refinement and wealth deceive no one; we must not look down on struggling Muslims elsewhere. A pre-Islamic poem about a man who could not avenge his brother against his own people shows we remain one ummah in strength and weakness. The goal is to reach a safe shore where you fear passing judgement on anyone and make your own story one you would not be ashamed to hear on the Day. The martyrdom of Haram ibn Milhan, whose killer later accepted Islam, shows even the Prophet could not see how stories end. A believer from Pharaoh's people warns Musa, who leaves Egypt, as later prophets left their lands, praying for rescue and guidance without complaint, ready to serve wherever Allah sends him. Along the way he discusses Madyan's location, the nature of tafsir encyclopedias, and fine points of recitation. At the well Musa asks the two women about their situation rather than judging, which yields rulings on women working and respectful conversation between the sexes. He helps, withdraws to the shade, and in one sentence praises, thanks and asks his Lord.

outline.heading: Recap: al-Qasas as the heart of the axis
outline.gist: The longest and most beautiful surah of the relationships axis, summarised in two principles about people's stories.

outline.heading: Judging springs from suspicion and superiority
outline.gist: Passing judgement usually assumes the worst and makes us feel better than others, yet every story reduces to a few simple diseases.

outline.heading: An onlooker would condemn a prophet
outline.gist: Seeing Musa strike a man dead, you would call him an aggressor, not knowing the victim was an oppressor and Musa a prophet.

outline.heading: Privilege could have made him an oppressor
outline.gist: Close to Pharaoh, Musa could have become chief of police or a minister over his own people.

outline.heading: A polished oppressor is still an oppressor
outline.gist: Wealth, calm manners and refinement do not change a tyrant, and the oppressed remain oppressed even if ill-mannered.

outline.heading: No right to side with criminals against my people
outline.gist: Being well educated gives no right to back oppressors because one's people are ignorant; do not look down on Muslims living in danger.

outline.heading: The pause before the second strike
outline.gist: This time Musa held back, and the enemy exposed the earlier killing.

outline.heading: Al-Harith ibn Wa'lah's dilemma
outline.gist: A pre-Islamic poet whose own people killed his brother found that striking back would only wound himself.

outline.heading: One ummah in victory and defeat
outline.gist: We stay one community in weakness too; if others will not teach our children, we must, with patience.

outline.heading: The false charge of being a tyrant
outline.gist: Musa's culture before prophethood surpassed ours; the Egyptian judged him a tyrant from one act and was wrong.

outline.heading: The safe shore: fearing to judge anyone
outline.gist: Reach a point where you fear saying a word about anyone; we are only stories, so make yours one you would not be ashamed of when told on the Day.

outline.heading: Bi'r Ma'unah: the Prophet cursed the killers by name
outline.gist: After the reciters were massacred he supplicated against named men in his prayers.

outline.heading: Haram ibn Milhan: 'I have won'
outline.gist: Stabbed from behind, he declared victory; his killer, puzzled by those words, later embraced Islam, showing no one can judge how a story ends.

outline.heading: Recitation: the warning and the flight
outline.gist: Heavy and light letters in the passage.

outline.heading: The believing man from Pharaoh's people
outline.gist: Pharaoh sought a pretext to kill Musa; the believer who concealed his faith came from the palace at the city's edge.

outline.heading: Running from the far end: the chiefs conspire
outline.gist: The man rushed because he loved Musa; the chiefs were seeking Pharaoh's order to kill him.

outline.heading: Leaving the land of his birth
outline.gist: Leaving the land of birth, family and memories was hard for Musa, for the Prophet and for Ibrahim; he told his family and left.

outline.heading: Fearful and watching: My Lord, save me
outline.gist: Expecting capture at any moment, he prayed to be saved from the wrongdoing people.

outline.heading: Where was Madyan, and was Shu'ayb there?
outline.gist: Most likely on the eastern Red Sea coast near Tabuk; whether Shu'ayb came before or after Musa is disputed; messengers were sent beyond the Israelites.

outline.heading: Madyan's lineage and differences among scholars
outline.gist: Reports trace Madyan to a son of Ibrahim by another wife; legitimate differences exist even on whether the sacrificed son was Isma'il or Ishaq.

outline.heading: Tafsir books are encyclopedias
outline.gist: Classical tafsirs collect everything said, sound or weak, and are not for lay reading; Ibn Ashur's work verifies reports and suits serious readers.

outline.heading: Genealogy and the mention of Ya'qub
outline.gist: The Arabs cared about Israelite lineages; naming Ya'qub with Ishaq seems meant to settle Ibrahim's descendants.

outline.heading: The journey: the sea on his right
outline.gist: With only a direction, he crossed Sinai barefoot and hungry for weeks.

outline.heading: His duas show he knew his Lord before prophethood
outline.gist: His words after the killing, his vow and his prayers for rescue and guidance reveal deep understanding.

outline.heading: 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me': a soul fit for prophethood
outline.gist: Not knowing whether the trip would take a day or a year, he hoped without complaint; he would be away for decades.

outline.heading: Ruined by his own side, yet no complaint
outline.gist: The man from his own people cost him home and family, and he lived as a refugee with no guarantee of return, yet he did not object to Allah.

outline.heading: Serving a purpose wherever he is sent
outline.gist: He trusted Allah's promise and moved as Allah eased his way.

outline.heading: Reciting the well verse and his licence exam
outline.gist: This verse is hard on the tongue; his teacher made him repeat it, and it is fine to slow down to give each letter its due.

outline.heading: At the water of Madyan: holding back the flock
outline.gist: People settle by fresh water; dhawd is used for livestock, so the two women were holding back their sheep.

outline.heading: He asked instead of judging
outline.gist: Keeping animals from water looks cruel and ill-mannered, but Musa asked what their situation was.

outline.heading: Why Musa was patient here but not with al-Khidr
outline.gist: He could be patient with people but struggled to understand acts embodying Allah's decree.

outline.heading: Waiting until the shepherds leave
outline.gist: They avoided crowding among the men and worked because their father was very old.

outline.heading: Rulings: women working
outline.gist: Women may earn by their own work, even in work mostly done by men when needed.

outline.heading: Respectful speech between men and women
outline.gist: A man may address women with modesty and good intent; such mixing is not sinful in itself.

outline.heading: Stopping on a doubled letter
outline.gist: When pausing on a doubled letter as in 'to the shade', make the doubling clear.

outline.heading: He watered for them and walked away
outline.gist: No lingering, chatting or asking for food; the whole scene is modesty and manners.

outline.heading: My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send
outline.gist: In one sentence he praises Allah, thanks Him for past good and asks for more, alone in a land where he knew no one.

outline.heading: Strength, courtesy and knowing when to speak
outline.gist: Strong enough to move a great rock, he still spoke only when needed and then turned to Allah; this is why such people are chosen.
